prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which opened a new regime of precision measurement.

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is the cleanest instance on the shortlist of a new regime being opened and then verified across laboratories. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift while many atoms stay confined in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and Ye's group took the strontium clock to the 1e-18 level and developed the many-body (spin-exchange and interaction) understanding that explains why the clock works. Independent groups with Sr and Yb now reproduce comparable performance, and comparisons between clocks resolve the gravitational redshift over millimetre scales and constrain drifts of constants. The attribution is natural for two people: concept and first realisation on one side, systematic accuracy and the many-body physics on the other. I move this to my first choice because, on reflection, it has the strongest combination of originality, reproducibility and a tight credit list.
statement.case_against: The main objection is novelty relative to the 2005 prize (frequency comb and precision spectroscopy) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, control of single trapped ions, with optical ion clocks as a showpiece). A sceptical member can call the lattice clock an extraordinary refinement of metrology rather than a new phenomenon. Credit is also not sealed: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and other Sr/Yb groups, and the ion-clock community, made contributions that two names cannot capture. Finally, the possible redefinition of the second is still pending, so the practical payoff is not yet realised.

responses.point: The lattice clock is a new measurement method that changed what can be measured, and Katori and Ye are the two decisive names.
responses.response: I agree on the core and on the two-person credit. Where I would add a qualification is the term 'method': the stronger argument is that the many-atom lattice clock showed collective and interaction effects (spin-exchange, many-body clock physics) that were not anticipated, so it is also a physics result and not only a metrology advance. That framing also helps against the objection that this is a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I still want us to say explicitly why the lattice clock is not simply the ion clock with better numbers, and I do not think the pending redefinition of the second should be used either as a reason to wait or as a reason to act.

responses.point: The Higgs observation (B054) is a decisive experimental discovery that completed the Standard Model, and the experiment has not yet been recognised although the theory was in 2013.
responses.response: I do not dispute the scientific weight of the Higgs discovery and defer to you and the particle physicists on its significance. My reservation is attribution rather than merit. Two collaborations of thousands means any three names are a judgement about leadership, and your own ballot shows the committee is split between Virdee and Della Negra for the CMS slot. With Katori and Ye the credit is close to unambiguous. I would put B054 high in a configuration discussion only if we can agree a defensible rule for naming three people from ATLAS and CMS, and I would like to hear whether you think such a rule exists.

responses.point: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (B019) reveal a class of quantum matter classified by band topology, and a theory-plus-experiment trio fits.
responses.response: This is a strong field and I rank it highly, but it is outside my core expertise and I am uneasy about the credit. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe quantum well, and Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Roy and Hasan's group are tied to the three-dimensional case, so the credited trio omits people whose contributions look decisive. The 2016 prize on topology in matter also makes some members see this as a neighbour. I would keep B019 as a serious alternative, but I would want to see an argument that the Z2 and quantum spin Hall step is distinct and that the credited trio is the right one before putting it ahead of the clock.

responses.point: IceCube (B033) is a detector-driven discovery that opened neutrino astronomy, with Halzen and Karle as the two names; the case should rest on the diffuse flux more than on TXS 0506+056.
responses.response: I agree that measurement craft over decades deserves weight, and I accept that the case rests on the diffuse flux, with the point-source evidence as supporting. Still, I would qualify the maturity: the origin of the diffuse flux is unresolved and the NGC 1068 and Galactic plane results are at modest significance, whereas the clock is verified at the 1e-18 level across several laboratories. I also remain concerned that the tight credit around Halzen and Karle underplays AMANDA, Baikal and other founders. I think both are serious, but I see the clock as the more mature case today.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
How much weight to give Lemonde, Takamoto and other lattice-clock contributors when only two names are credited.
Whether circuit QED (B001) should be held back because the 2025 prize recognised superconducting circuits, or whether that is a point for rather than against it.
I am recalling priority and chronology details from memory and have not verified them against the original papers.
statement.conflict_note: Circuit QED (B001), which I ranked first in the opening, is the architecture my own research and the WACQT programme I direct are built on, and its credited names (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf) are close colleagues and collaborators in the field. I flag a possible recusal issue for B001 and for any configuration containing it, and I therefore weight B048 here. I have no specific connection to Katori or Ye apparent from my profile.
